transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Well, what finally made me agree to come in is that I just... I don't care about the things that used to keep me balanced. I used to love sailing races, and I had a Saturday shift at the historical society, but now... even tinkering in the woodshop just feels like a chore. I just keep putting it all off.
How long have you been feeling this way—when did you first notice you stopped caring about sailing, the historical society, and woodworking?

It's been a little over a year now. It all started right after... well, there was a scaffold accident at work during a business readjustment phase. That's really when I first noticed I just didn't have the drive for any of it anymore.
Since the accident, have you been having any unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about it that intrude on your mind even when you don't want them to?

Yeah, I do. Sometimes, out of nowhere, I'll just... I'll see that scaffold dropping in my head. It's as clear as a photo. It happens especially if I hear a loud metal clank, or like a backup alarm on a truck outside. When it happens, for a few minutes, it's just really hard to stay focused on whatever meeting or conversation I'm actually in.
Since the accident, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, sounds, or conversations that remind you of what happened?

Yeah, I have. I've actually gotten very good at routing my day so I don't have to go anywhere near that coastal site, or even the harbor walkways by the cranes. And at work, if I'm in a conversation where someone starts replaying what went wrong that day... I just find a reason to step away or change the subject. I really just prefer to avoid it entirely.
Over this past year, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or empty most of the day, nearly every day?

No, I wouldn't really say that. I don't feel sad or down all day, every day. I mean... I've definitely lost my interest in things, like I mentioned, but I don't walk around feeling empty or depressed. I still get up, go to work, and manage my projects. So no, it's not a constant sadness.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient developed symptoms following a life-threatening scaffold accident approximately 13 months ago, with a clear temporal link between a traumatic stressor and symptom onset. Core PTSD symptom clusters are present: intrusive re-experiencing (vivid, unbidden images of the accident triggered by sensory cues like loud clanks/alarms), avoidance behaviors (routing around the accident site, avoiding conversations about the event), and negative alterations in mood/interest (loss of interest in previously valued activities—sailing, historical society, woodworking). Symptoms have persisted well beyond one month, satisfying duration criteria. Major depressive disorder is less likely given the patient explicitly denies persistent depressed or empty mood, despite anhedonia. Adjustment disorder (F43.2) is a candidate but is less fitting given the specific intrusion/avoidance symptom clusters clearly tied to a traumatic (not merely stressful) event and the chronicity (>1 year) exceeding typical adjustment disorder presentations.
